articles.headline: The Guardian view on ‘two-tier policing’: tackle the myth, don’t pander to it | Editorial
articles.teaser: Confidence in the system is being corroded by cynical campaigns and far-right propaganda – that is the challenge to be confrontedThere are many areas of policy where public opinion diverges from evidence. The challenge is to find methods of persuasion that don’t belittle the experiences of people who are afraid, and don’t like to be told their fears are unfounded.But there is a different challenge that arises when the cause of public concern is a problem that doesn’t really exist.

articles.headline: What stops us building the houses Britain needs | Letters
articles.teaser: Emeritus professor Simon Price, Smart Growth UK’s Jon Reeds and former Labour council leader Steve Siddon respond to a column by John Harris John Harris points out the utter inadequacy of Labour’s housing plans, despite Andy Burnham’s passionate advocacy for new social housing (Is Burnham’s plan for a housing revolution anything more than a pipedream?, 15 November). And everyone agrees that we need many more houses. So what’s holding us back?The problem lies in the fiscal rules. articles.originalHeadline: What stops us building the houses Britain needs | Letters

articles.headline: BMI was never meant to evaluate an individual’s health | Letter
articles.teaser: Clinicians should start with the patient in front of them to identify obesity, not rely on a 200-year-old method that was aimed at entire populations, says James CaponYour report on a better way to diagnose obesity is welcome, though it is worth remembering how we came to rely on body mass index (BMI) in the first place (BMI alternative for identifying obesity ‘could prevent misdiagnosis in millions’, 11 November).The index was devised in the 1830s by the Belgian statistician Adolphe Quetelet, who wanted to describe the “average man” across whole populations. He never intended it as a verdict on any individual’s health, and it was largely forgotten until 1972, when the American physiologist Ancel Keys, most famous for developing the diet-heart hypothesis, revived it and gave it its current name. Again, it was for population studies. Continue reading...
articles.originalHeadline: BMI was never meant to evaluate an individual’s health | Letter

articles.headline: Why Palantir’s health tech is not the right fit for the NHS | Letter
articles.teaser: The US firm’s health data system is based on an insurance model of healthcare, not the patient-centred universal service we have in Britain, says Prof Caroline MitchellThe news that NHS England may have overstated the benefits of Palantir for improving efficiency will surprise few frontline clinicians (NHS England deletes ‘misleading’ claim 137 trusts benefiting from Palantir AI tools, 12 November)Too often, global digital policy assumes that software designed for the fragmented, insurance-based US healthcare system can simply be adapted to a universal public service elsewhere. A legitimate concern is that algorithms underpinning AI decision-making may be immature in the NHS context, having been developed primarily for a very different US healthcare system. Continue reading...
articles.originalHeadline: Why Palantir’s health tech is not the right fit for the NHS | Letter

articles.headline: Blaming Ofsted inspectors for the system is unfair | Letters
articles.teaser: Inspectors and educators alike have been placed under even greater pressure year after year, says Helen KennyAs national officer for the FDA, the union representing a large number of His Majesty’s Inspectors (HMIs), I read Simon Jenkins’ piece with great interest (Ofsted’s menacing inspections are still disastrous. Schools should answer to the communities they serve, 13 November). Jenkins dismisses the work of HMIs as merely a “sniff” of the air and a stroll back to Whitehall, showing a lack of knowledge about their role. HMIs are former school leaders, with a deep knowledge and dedication to educating children and young people.

This week my Instagram feed has been full of female friends, colleagues and acquaintances sharing his words: “Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no and to demand justice from the criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Russell Brand, act without their consent.” Those same women are now sharing the Guardian and ITV’s investigation into David Walliams, who is accused of preying on young women for sex, with the same fury and fervour (Walliams has denied the allegations against him).Both of these stories concerning predatory male behaviour took place in an era when I was a young woman: the “lad culture” era. It dated from about the mid-to-late 90s until the beginning of the #MeToo movement in 2016, and those of us who came of age during it sometimes joke bleakly that it’s a miracle we made it out in one piece. Some of us didn’t, and those victim-survivors live with the daily impact of male coercion, abuse and violence, still.
articles.originalHeadline: Why did it take so long to unmask Brand and Walliams? Because noughties culture told girls like me abuse was normal | Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett

articles.headline: For Trump, Musk and Farage, the message is the same: voters don’t want to be hijacked by billionaires | Rafael Behr
articles.teaser: A lesson from the US midterms is that electorates are repelled by the arrogant mega-rich buying democracy. This is a fight Labour can afford to pick For most people, $224m (£168m) is a lot of money, especially if you spend it and get nothing in return. But Elon Musk is richer than most people. In fact, there is no one richer.As the wealthiest of the US’s tech oligarchs Musk could afford to blow huge sums on a failed bid to prop up Republican candidates in Texas, his adoptive home state, in last week’s midterm congressional elections.
articles.originalHeadline: For Trump, Musk and Farage, the message is the same: voters don’t want to be hijacked by billionaires | Rafael Behr

articles.headline: Why Michael Gove worries about Britishness | Radical Thinking with Aditya Chakrabortty
articles.teaser: For more than three decades, Michael Gove has been a leading figure in British Conservatism. As a journalist, government minister and now editor of the Tory bible, the Spectator, he has helped shape the right even as it has moved further rightwards. In the latest episode of Radical Thinking, Gove joins Aditya Chakrabortty to discuss the future of the right, his record on Brexit and austerity, and the Spectator’s position on Islam.Aditya’s suggested reading:To read the fruits of Michael Gove’s dalliance with the Marxism Today gang, look up his essay in a 1998 collection called The Moderniser’s Dilemma: Radical Politics in the Age of Blair.For a slalom ride through Michael Gove’s years in power, read The Demented Dalek by the historian Richard J Evans in the London Review of Books.To learn more about what’s become of the British right, there’s a column by me for the Guardian.Phil Burton-Cartledge examines why Britain's most successful political party is now failing in his book The Party’s Over: The Rise and Fall of the Conservatives from Thatcher to Sunak.Phil also writes a very good blog on British politics, which keeps a close eye on how each party is trying to marshal a coalition of voters. Here he is on Kemi Badenoch.Geoffrey Wheatcroft offers an entertaining short narrative in Bloody Panico!: or, Whatever Happened to The Tory PartyFor more on the economics of the Cameron years, this paper examines how the Tories failed to move the UK away from being a country of renters towards a country of makers.
